[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is highly specific: a young woman with *intermittent, eating-triggered shooting otalgia* 12 weeks after tympanoplasty, localized to the right ear, and exacerbated by earrings — all classic features of **Arnold’s neuralgia** (also known as *auricular branch of the vagus nerve neuralgia* or *vagus nerve auricular neuralgia*). The temporal relationship to surgery strongly implicates iatrogenic injury — such as traction, compression, or neuroma formation — along the course of the auricular branch (CN X), which innervates the concha, posterior external auditory canal (EAC), and posteroinferior pinna. Eating triggers pain because swallowing activates the pharyngeal plexus (also vagal), leading to cross-activation or ephaptic transmission in an injured or sensitized auricular branch. The absence of cranial nerve VII–VIII–IX/X deficits rules out broader pathology (e.g., glomus tumor, neurovascular compression at the jugular foramen, or central lesion) and supports a *peripheral, focal neuropathic process*. The diagnostic lidocaine block of Arnold’s nerve is definitive: transient abolition of pain confirms the diagnosis. Imaging priorities are appropriately targeted to identify structural irritants (e.g., bony spicules, granulation tissue, or small neuroma) near the nerve’s peripheral course — not the cerebellopontine angle (where vagal root entry zone lesions would present with different symptoms). Stapedius reflex and audiometry are prudent to exclude subtle facial nerve involvement or middle ear sequelae, but their normal results would further reinforce the peripheral vagal branch localization.

- Clinical suspicion explicitly points to iatrogenic irritation or neuroma of the auricular branch of the vagus nerve near the posterior EAC — a well-documented postsurgical complication.
